questions.q: In the suvat equations, what do the five letters s, u, v, a and t stand for?
options: Speed, units, velocity, area and time
Displacement, initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration and time
Distance, velocity, average velocity, acceleration and time
Displacement, velocity, final velocity, area under graph and time
questions.explanation: Suvat is the memory hook for the five quantities: s is displacement, u the initial velocity, v the final velocity, a the (constant) acceleration and t the time. The tempting slip is calling u and v 'speed' — they are velocities, vectors that carry signs.

questions.q: Which equation of uniformly accelerated motion does NOT contain displacement (s)?
options: \(v = u + at\)
\(s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2\)
questions.explanation: Each of the four equations omits exactly one quantity: \(v=u+at\) has no s, \(s=ut+\tfrac12 at^2\) has no v, \(v^2=u^2+2as\) has no t, and \(s=\tfrac12(u+v)t\) has no a. You choose by spotting the quantity that is neither given nor wanted.

questions.q: A car accelerates from 10 m s⁻¹ to 30 m s⁻¹ over 100 m and you are asked for the acceleration. Using the missing-variable method, which equation should you reach for?
options: \(v = u + at\), because time is given
\(s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2\), because final velocity is missing
\(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\), because time is the missing quantity
\(s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u+v)t\), because acceleration is missing
questions.explanation: You are given u, v and s and asked for a, so the quantity that is neither given nor asked for is t — the time. The equation with no t is \(v^2=u^2+2as\). The missing quantity points you straight to the right equation, no guessing.

questions.q: At the very highest point of a ball thrown straight up, what are its velocity and its acceleration?
options: Velocity is zero and acceleration is zero
Velocity is zero and acceleration is g (≈9.8 m s⁻²) downward
Velocity is maximum and acceleration is zero
Velocity is g downward and acceleration is zero
questions.explanation: At the top the ball is momentarily at rest, so v = 0, but gravity never switches off — the acceleration is still 9.8 m s⁻² downward. The classic trap is assuming zero velocity means zero acceleration; if that were true the ball would hang there instead of falling back.

questions.q: When you take 'up' as the positive direction for a thrown ball, how should the acceleration due to gravity be signed?
options: Positive, because the ball is moving
Negative, because gravity points down while up is positive
Zero, because gravity only acts at the top of the flight
Positive on the way up and negative on the way down
questions.explanation: Once you choose up as positive you must apply that convention to every quantity: gravity points down, so a = −9.8 m s⁻² for the whole flight. Making g positive when up is positive is the single most common sign error and gives nonsensical answers like a negative height.

questions.q: From memory: state the four-step missing-variable method for choosing and using a suvat equation.
keyPoints: Write down suvat — the five letters — as a list.
Fill in the three values you are given, with their signs, using your chosen positive direction.
Identify the quantity you are asked to find and the one quantity that is neither given nor asked for (the missing one).
Choose the equation that does NOT contain that missing quantity, then substitute and solve.
questions.explanation: If you recalled all four steps and that you select the equation lacking the missing variable, grade yourself Good or Easy. The whole game is: every problem hands you three quantities, asks for a fourth, and leaves one out.

questions.q: In your own words: why do the four equations of motion only apply when the acceleration is constant, and how does this make them perfect for motion under gravity?
keyPoints: Uniformly accelerated motion means constant acceleration; the equations come straight from a straight-line velocity-time graph (constant gradient).
If the acceleration changes during the motion, no single equation applies to the whole journey — you must break it into segments where a is constant.
Near Earth's surface (ignoring air resistance) every object falls with constant acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻² downward, so suvat is tailor-made for motion under gravity.
questions.explanation: If you linked 'constant acceleration' to both the limitation and the free-fall application, mark it Good or Easy. The equations are the velocity-time graph written as algebra, so they need the straight line that constant acceleration gives.

questions.q: A car accelerates from 10 m s⁻¹ to 30 m s⁻¹ over a distance of 100 m. Calculate its (constant) acceleration.
questions.explanation: Time is the missing quantity, so the equation with no t — \(v^2=u^2+2as\) — is the one to use. Write the equation, substitute with units, rearrange and solve; the marker rewards each step.

questions.q: A ball is thrown straight up at 20 m s⁻¹. Taking up as positive and g = 9.8 m s⁻² downward, calculate the maximum height it reaches.
questions.given: \(u = +20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\),  \(v = 0\) (momentarily at rest at the top),  \(a = -9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\); t is missing, find \(s\)
questions.explanation: The key insight is that at the top the velocity is momentarily zero, which gives you the third known. Time is missing, so use \(v^2=u^2+2as\) with a negative because up is positive. Making g positive here would give a nonsensical negative height.

questions.q: Explain why the four equations of motion can be applied to an object in free fall under gravity, but cannot be applied to a car whose acceleration is increasing. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: The four equations of uniformly accelerated motion are valid only when the acceleration is constant. An object in free fall near the Earth's surface, ignoring air resistance, has a constant acceleration equal to g (about 9.8 m s⁻² downward), so the equations apply directly to its motion. A car whose acceleration is increasing does not have constant acceleration, so the equations cannot be applied to its motion as a whole; you would have to break the motion into intervals over which the acceleration is approximately constant.

criteria.descriptor: States that the equations require constant (uniform) acceleration.
Explains that free fall has constant acceleration g, so the equations apply.
Explains that the car's increasing acceleration violates the condition, so the equations cannot be applied to the whole motion.

questions.explanation: This tests whether you know the limitation, not just the formulas. The crux is the contrast between constant acceleration (free fall) and changing acceleration (the car).
